description: I'm a student interested in space, technology, and building things that solve real problems. I regularly participate in hackathons, where I enjoy turning ideas into working projects. I created Nova's Moon Mission to combine my interest in space exploration and programming into an interactive game that makes the challenges of living on the Moon easier for younger players to understand.
summary:
Nova's Moon Mission is a 10-day lunar-base management game designed to help children understand what it takes to sustain a human settlement on the Moon.

Players take charge of a small crew and manage the base's power, water, oxygen, and safety. They must decide how to use limited energy, whether to prioritize science or essential systems, and how to prepare for solar storms.

The game uses real NASA space-weather records from DONKI to create its storm scenarios, alongside real space-biology research from NASA's OSDR to introduce the challenges of growing plants in space.

I wanted to make these ideas easier for younger audiences to understand. Instead of only reading about space exploration, players get to make the decisions themselves and see how their choices affect the crew and the mission.
details:
Project Details

Nova's Moon Mission – Project Solution

Nova's Moon Mission is an interactive browser game where children get to manage their own Moon base for 10 days. Players take care of a crew of astronauts, manage limited resources, and make decisions to keep the mission running. The game brings real NASA space-weather data and space-biology research into gameplay, helping younger players explore some of the challenges of living on the Moon.

How Does Our Solution Work?

At the beginning, players choose between two locations for their lunar base: a polar ridge or an equatorial plain. Each location has different advantages and challenges, especially when it comes to power availability and scientific research.

Every day, players receive a limited number of power chips and decide how to distribute them across the base's systems. They can drag power chips onto different machines and activities, then end the day to see how their choices affect the crew and their supplies.

  • Power Management: Players distribute their available power between systems such as the radio, water cleaner, oxygen maker, greenhouse, laboratory, shields, and solar panels. They can also store unused power in a battery or build additional solar panels to increase their supply.
  • Water and Oxygen: The water cleaner uses power to reduce water loss, while the oxygen maker needs both water and power to produce oxygen. Players have to keep these systems running to make sure the crew has enough essential supplies.
  • Greenhouse and Science: The greenhouse uses water and power but provides oxygen and science points. Players can also send crew members outside for scientific research, earning science points while increasing their exposure to environmental risks.
  • Solar Storms: Players encounter solar storms based on real space-weather records. They can use the radio to receive warnings and build shields to reduce the crew's exposure. During a storm, they must decide whether to keep the crew inside or send them outside for research.
  • Delayed Consequences: Some decisions don't cause problems immediately. Certain events create costs that appear a few days later. For example, neglecting the water cleaner can eventually leave the base with too little water.

The mission lasts 10 days. To win, players must keep the crew safe, maintain enough water and oxygen, and reach the required science target. Running out of water or oxygen, or allowing crew risk to reach the failure threshold, ends the mission.

How NASA Data Is Used

I used these datasets to make the game actually educational:

  • NASA DONKI: The game retrieves real solar-flare and coronal mass ejection (CME) records through NASA's DONKI API. These records help determine the severity of the game's storm events. CME speed is also used in a simplified calculation to estimate warning time, while the radio determines whether players receive the full warning.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): The game features real space-biology studies, including research on plants grown in lunar soil, plants grown aboard the International Space Station, and radiation-related biological changes. These studies give players a look at the research behind growing plants and understanding radiation in space.
  • NASA Image and Video Library: NASA images are used in the game's information cards and visual content to help players explore real space environments.

Some values, such as resource amounts, storm exposure, and science points, are simplified game mechanics rather than actual NASA measurements.

The Game Benefits

Children, students, and anyone interested in space exploration by:

  • Introducing younger players to the challenges of living and working on the Moon.
  • Helping them understand how power, water, oxygen, and crew safety depend on one another.
  • Showing how limited resources create trade-offs and why planning ahead matters.
  • Connecting interactive gameplay with real NASA data and scientific research.
  • Making space science easier to explore through hands-on decisions rather than just reading information.
  • Introduce new words related to space.

My Goal

My goal is to make the challenges of living on the Moon easier for younger children to understand and explore. Instead of simply reading about how astronauts might survive beyond Earth, players get to manage a lunar base themselves and experience how their decisions affect the entire mission. I also wanted to show how NASA's open data and research can be used in ways that make space science more accessible and interesting.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages and Frameworks:

  • JavaScript and TypeScript → for the game's functionality and simulation.
  • React 19 and Vite → for building the browser-based application.
  • Phaser 3 → for the interactive game environment.

AI Tools:

  • Google Gemini → used to create the game's artwork.
  • Leonardo AI → used to generate visual assets.
  • Cursor → used for AI-assisted coding and development.

NASA Data Sources:

  • NASA DONKI API → solar-flare and coronal mass ejection records.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) → space-biology research.
  • NASA Image and Video Library → NASA images used in the game.

Other Technologies:

  • SQLite → used for storing simulation data.
  • Backend API routes → retrieve NASA data without making direct API requests from the browser.
